name: arc_shapes
description: Book- and chapter-scale shapes for the reader's line of feeling or belief: story arcs (valence = fortune or emotion) and epistemic arcs (valence = certainty, -1 doubt to +1 conviction). Optional 'curve' is [[position 0-1, valence -1..1], ...].

vonnegut_shapes.name: man in hole
vonnegut_shapes.definition: A protagonist in decent shape falls into trouble and climbs out of it, ending higher than where they began.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: Gives the reader the pleasure of recovery; the ending reads as earned rather than given.
vonnegut_shapes.caution: The most-used commercial shape there is; if the hole costs the protagonist nothing, the climb reads as a formality.

vonnegut_shapes.name: boy meets girl
vonnegut_shapes.definition: An ordinary person finds something wonderful, loses it, and gets it back.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: The loss in the middle converts a want into a need, so the recovery lands harder than the discovery.
vonnegut_shapes.register: fiction; the backbone of romance and of most acquisition plots

vonnegut_shapes.name: from bad to worse
vonnegut_shapes.definition: A protagonist who starts badly off is driven steadily further down with no reprieve.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: Produces dread rather than suspense: the question is not whether but how far.
vonnegut_shapes.caution: Without variation in the rate of descent the line goes numb; readers stop registering a drop they have already priced in.

vonnegut_shapes.name: which way is up
vonnegut_shapes.definition: The line refuses to resolve because the audience is never reliably told whether what happens is good news or bad.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: Trades catharsis for verisimilitude — Vonnegut's point being that this is the shape of actual life.
vonnegut_shapes.caution: Requires a compensating engine (voice, ideas, texture); ambiguity alone will not hold a reader for 300 pages.

vonnegut_shapes.name: creation story
vonnegut_shapes.definition: Fortune rises in discrete gifts from nothing to plenty, each step a bestowal rather than an achievement.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: Reads as cosmology or institutional history rather than drama, because nothing is contested.
vonnegut_shapes.register: myth, origin stories, company and field histories

vonnegut_shapes.name: old testament
vonnegut_shapes.definition: A stepwise ascent to a height followed by a single catastrophic fall.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: The accumulated gifts become the measure of the loss; the higher the ladder, the deeper the drop.

vonnegut_shapes.name: new testament
vonnegut_shapes.definition: Stepwise ascent, catastrophic fall, then a final rise that goes off the top of the scale.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: The transcendent close reframes the catastrophe as necessary, which is why the shape carries religious and redemptive material.
vonnegut_shapes.caution: The off-scale ending is the hardest beat in fiction to earn; unearned it reads as authorial rescue.

vonnegut_shapes.name: cinderella
vonnegut_shapes.definition: Stepwise rise, sudden collapse at the moment of greatest happiness, then a rise past the earlier peak.
vonnegut_shapes.effect: Vonnegut's claim was that this is the most popular shape ever devised, and the audience data since has not embarrassed him.

rise_and_fall_families.name: rags to riches
rise_and_fall_families.definition: A monotonic rise in fortune from deprivation to fulfilment.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: Satisfies aspiration directly; the risk is that a line with no descent has no suspense.
rise_and_fall_families.caution: Needs local setbacks inside the rise or it reads as a résumé.

rise_and_fall_families.name: riches to rags
rise_and_fall_families.definition: A monotonic fall from fortune to ruin.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: Reads as inevitability; the reader watches for the cause rather than the outcome.

rise_and_fall_families.name: icarus
rise_and_fall_families.definition: A rise to a peak followed by a fall caused by the rise itself.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: Makes the ascent and the descent the same act, which is what separates it from mere misfortune.

rise_and_fall_families.name: oedipus
rise_and_fall_families.definition: A fall, a recovery, and a second deeper fall.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: The middle recovery is what makes the second fall unbearable: the reader was allowed to hope.

rise_and_fall_families.name: fortune's wheel
rise_and_fall_families.definition: Rise and fall presented as the impersonal turning of fortune rather than as consequence of character.
rise_and_fall_families.register: medieval and early modern narrative; still live in journalism about markets and dynasties
rise_and_fall_families.caution: Because the turn is impersonal, agency drains out of the story; use it for panorama, not for a single protagonist.

rise_and_fall_families.name: de casibus fall
rise_and_fall_families.definition: The fall of an eminent person from prosperity to misery, told as an admonitory case.
rise_and_fall_families.register: moralized biography, corporate post-mortems, downfall reporting

rise_and_fall_families.name: fall from grace
rise_and_fall_families.definition: A descent measured in moral standing rather than material fortune.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: The reader's judgement, not the character's circumstances, supplies the downward pressure.

rise_and_fall_families.name: reversal of fortune
rise_and_fall_families.definition: A shape organized around one hinge at which the line crosses zero and the situation inverts.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: Concentrates all structural weight on a single scene, which must therefore be the best scene in the book.

rise_and_fall_families.name: comic mythos
rise_and_fall_families.definition: Frye's spring shape: an obstructing order is overturned and a new society forms around the young protagonists.
rise_and_fall_families.register: comedy from Menander to the romantic comedy; also the shape of most reform arguments

rise_and_fall_families.name: romantic mythos
rise_and_fall_families.definition: Frye's summer shape: the quest — perilous journey, crucial struggle, exaltation of the hero.

rise_and_fall_families.name: tragic mythos
rise_and_fall_families.definition: Frye's autumn shape: the hero is isolated from society and falls.

rise_and_fall_families.name: ironic mythos
rise_and_fall_families.definition: Frye's winter shape: bondage, frustration and absurdity, with a protagonist weaker than the reader.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: Denies the reader both triumph and catharsis; the pleasure on offer is recognition.

rise_and_fall_families.name: circular return
rise_and_fall_families.definition: The line ends at the condition it started from, with only the reader's understanding changed.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: Converts plot into pattern: the meaning is in what the repetition now looks like.
rise_and_fall_families.caution: If nothing but position returns, the book reads as a wasted trip; something in the reader must be different.

rise_and_fall_families.name: double reversal
rise_and_fall_families.definition: A complex plot with two hinges, so the outcome inverts and then inverts again.
rise_and_fall_families.effect: The standard comic engine: two characters' fortunes trade places, then trade back on new terms.
rise_and_fall_families.caution: Three or more reversals and the reader stops investing in any of them.

epistemic_arcs.name: delayed thesis
epistemic_arcs.definition: The claim is withheld until late, so the reader travels the evidence before being told what it means.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Disarms a hostile reader, who cannot start refuting a thesis that has not yet been stated.
epistemic_arcs.register: essay, op-ed for resistant audiences, literary nonfiction
epistemic_arcs.caution: Requires a strong non-thesis engine early — narrative, anomaly, or voice — or the reader leaves before the payoff.

epistemic_arcs.name: deductive descent
epistemic_arcs.definition: The thesis is stated first and certainty is spent unpacking its consequences downward into cases.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Maximum clarity, minimum suspense; the reader always knows where they are.
epistemic_arcs.register: technical writing, legal memoranda, executive prose

epistemic_arcs.name: inductive ascent
epistemic_arcs.definition: Particulars accumulate until a generalization becomes the only reasonable summary of them.
epistemic_arcs.caution: Certainty must rise strictly less fast than the evidence warrants; overclaiming at 0.5 costs the reader at 1.0.

epistemic_arcs.name: reductio ad absurdum
epistemic_arcs.definition: The opposing claim is granted and followed until it produces a contradiction or an intolerable consequence.
epistemic_arcs.effect: The reader does the refuting; the writer only supplies the road.
epistemic_arcs.caution: Fails outright if the opponent can accept the 'absurd' consequence, so test the terminus before building the road.

epistemic_arcs.name: converging proof
epistemic_arcs.definition: Several independent lines of evidence, each individually weak, are run to the same conclusion.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Certainty rises multiplicatively rather than additively because the failure modes are uncorrelated.
epistemic_arcs.caution: Only works if the lines really are independent; say so explicitly, because readers assume they are not.

epistemic_arcs.name: socratic elenchus
epistemic_arcs.definition: The interlocutor's confident answer is dismantled by questioning until the confidence is gone.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Ends lower than it began: the deliverable is refutation of a false belief, not a new one.

epistemic_arcs.name: aporetic arc
epistemic_arcs.definition: Every candidate answer is tried and found wanting, and the piece closes in acknowledged impasse.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Makes the difficulty of the question the finding, which is honest and rarely publishable in business contexts.
epistemic_arcs.caution: Distinguish an earned aporia from a failure to do the work; show the eliminations.

epistemic_arcs.name: paradigm shift
epistemic_arcs.definition: Settled consensus is disturbed by an anomaly, drifts into crisis, and is replaced by a new framework.
epistemic_arcs.register: intellectual history, science writing, industry-disruption argument
epistemic_arcs.caution: Overused as a flattering frame for ordinary incremental results.

epistemic_arcs.name: methodic doubt
epistemic_arcs.definition: Beliefs are suspended deliberately and to the maximum, then rebuilt from whatever survives.
epistemic_arcs.effect: The destruction phase buys credibility for the reconstruction phase.

epistemic_arcs.name: dialectical spiral
epistemic_arcs.definition: A position and its opposition are each pressed until a third position supersedes both, then the cycle repeats at a higher level.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Every synthesis is provisional, which lets a long argument keep moving without recanting.

epistemic_arcs.name: abductive arc
epistemic_arcs.definition: A surprising fact is presented, candidate explanations are ranked, and the best one is adopted provisionally.
epistemic_arcs.caution: Ends short of certainty by design; a curve that terminates at 1.0 has smuggled in a deduction.

epistemic_arcs.name: conjecture and refutation
epistemic_arcs.definition: A bold hypothesis is stated, exposed to the hardest available test, and either survives or is discarded for the next conjecture.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Certainty is always corrigible; the credibility comes from the severity of the tests, not the strength of the claim.

epistemic_arcs.name: consilience
epistemic_arcs.definition: Inductions from unrelated domains jump together on one explanation, and the coincidence is itself the argument.
epistemic_arcs.caution: The jump has to be genuine; separate fields agreeing because they share a source is not consilience.

epistemic_arcs.name: genealogical critique
epistemic_arcs.definition: A concept taken as natural is traced to its contingent origins, and the tracing erodes its authority.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Destabilizes without refuting: the claim was never shown false, only shown made.

epistemic_arcs.name: hermeneutics of suspicion
epistemic_arcs.definition: The surface account is treated as a disguise and read for the interest it conceals.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Confidence returns at the end but attaches to the unmasked motive rather than the stated one.
epistemic_arcs.caution: Unfalsifiable if applied uniformly; specify what evidence would show the surface account was simply true.

epistemic_arcs.name: hermeneutic circle
epistemic_arcs.definition: Understanding oscillates between part and whole, each pass revising the other, until the readings stabilize.
epistemic_arcs.effect: Models interpretive work honestly — the wobble in the curve is the argument's method showing.

epistemic_arcs.name: via negativa
epistemic_arcs.definition: The subject is approached by eliminating what it is not, the residue standing in for a definition that cannot be given directly.
epistemic_arcs.register: theology, definition essays, writing about things resistant to definition
epistemic_arcs.caution: The eliminations must be exhaustive enough that the residue is small; otherwise the close is a shrug.

tension_curves.name: try-fail cycle
tension_curves.definition: The protagonist attempts a solution, fails in a way that worsens the position, and attempts again.
tension_curves.effect: Sawtooth descent: each partial recovery makes the next drop measurable.
tension_curves.caution: Three cycles is the conventional ceiling; a fourth failure teaches the reader the protagonist cannot win.

tension_curves.name: no-and escalation
tension_curves.definition: Each attempt is answered 'no, and something worse happens', so failure compounds rather than merely repeating.
tension_curves.effect: Distinguishes escalation from repetition; the 'and' is what raises the line's slope.

tension_curves.name: scene-sequel rhythm
tension_curves.definition: Alternation of goal-conflict-disaster scenes with reaction-dilemma-decision sequels.
tension_curves.effect: The sequels give the reader somewhere to put the last disaster before the next arrives.
tension_curves.caution: Skipping sequels for pace produces action the reader cannot feel; skipping scenes produces a book of reactions.

tension_curves.name: ticking clock
tension_curves.definition: A stated deadline converts every subsequent event into a cost against remaining time.
tension_curves.effect: Raises baseline tension without adding incident, which is why it rescues sagging middles.
tension_curves.caution: The clock must be visible and honestly kept; a deadline that slips silently retires the device for the rest of the book.

tension_curves.name: escalating stakes
tension_curves.definition: The magnitude of what can be lost is raised in steps, each step retroactively shrinking the last.
tension_curves.caution: Escalation to planetary stakes usually lowers tension, because the reader can no longer picture the loss.

tension_curves.name: tension and release
tension_curves.definition: Deliberate alternation of pressure and relief, so the reader's capacity to feel pressure is renewed.
tension_curves.effect: Unrelieved tension flattens into noise; the release is what makes the next rise measurable.

tension_curves.name: suspense curve
tension_curves.definition: The audience is given information the characters lack, and the tension is the wait for the collision.
tension_curves.effect: Hitchcock's distinction: telling the reader early buys minutes of dread instead of a second of shock.

tension_curves.name: surprise reversal
tension_curves.definition: Information is withheld and released at the turn, spending the tension in one spike.
tension_curves.caution: Pays once and only if the reader can reread the setup and find it fair.

tension_curves.name: double climax
tension_curves.definition: Two peaks — usually the external problem and the internal one — resolved in sequence rather than together.
tension_curves.caution: The second peak must be the one the book is actually about, or the ending reads as an appendix.

tension_curves.name: anticlimax
tension_curves.definition: Built tension is released into something deliberately smaller than promised.
tension_curves.effect: Used knowingly it is a statement about the world; used accidentally it is the commonest structural failure there is.

tension_curves.name: false resolution
tension_curves.definition: The problem appears solved with substantial text remaining, so the reader's relief becomes a source of dread.
tension_curves.caution: Needs enough remaining page count to be visible as a trick, or it reads as a botched ending.

tension_curves.name: cliffhanger chain
tension_curves.definition: Each unit ends on an unresolved turn that is answered only after the next unit has opened its own.
tension_curves.caution: Answers deferred too long stop being promises and start being debts the reader writes off.

tension_curves.name: slow burn
tension_curves.definition: Tension is raised so gradually that no single increment is visible, and the reader notices only the accumulated pressure.
tension_curves.effect: Produces unease rather than excitement; the payoff is the reader's realization of how far the line has moved.
tension_curves.caution: Requires compensating pleasures at every page, because nothing is happening quickly enough to carry the reader alone.

emotional_trajectories.name: positive change arc
emotional_trajectories.definition: The protagonist holds a lie about themselves or the world, is pressured by the truth, and ends by embracing it.
emotional_trajectories.effect: The standard change arc: internal movement supplies meaning while external plot supplies motion.

emotional_trajectories.name: flat arc
emotional_trajectories.definition: The protagonist already holds the truth and does not change; the world around them changes instead.
emotional_trajectories.effect: Puts the burden of transformation on the supporting cast, which is why it suits series and mentors.
emotional_trajectories.caution: A flat protagonist with a flat world is not an arc, it is a report.

emotional_trajectories.name: disillusionment arc
emotional_trajectories.definition: The protagonist believes a comforting lie, learns the truth, and the truth is worse.
emotional_trajectories.effect: Ends in clear sight and lost comfort; the gain is knowledge, the cost is everything else.

emotional_trajectories.name: fall arc
emotional_trajectories.definition: The protagonist clings to the lie, rejects the truth on offer, and is destroyed by the choice.
emotional_trajectories.caution: The truth must be genuinely available and genuinely refused, or the fall is misfortune rather than tragedy.

emotional_trajectories.name: corruption arc
emotional_trajectories.definition: The protagonist starts with the truth, is offered the lie, and takes it.
emotional_trajectories.effect: The reader's complicity is the engine: each step is individually defensible.

emotional_trajectories.name: redemption arc
emotional_trajectories.definition: A character who has done real harm pays a real cost and earns a changed standing.
emotional_trajectories.caution: Redemption granted without cost is the cheapest move in fiction; price it in what the character cannot get back.

emotional_trajectories.name: descent into madness
emotional_trajectories.definition: Perception degrades progressively until the narrated world and the actual world separate.
emotional_trajectories.effect: Runs on narration rather than event: the prose has to decay with the mind.

emotional_trajectories.name: innocence to experience
emotional_trajectories.definition: A protected worldview is broken by contact with the world and reassembled with the damage included.

emotional_trajectories.name: kubler-ross grief curve
emotional_trajectories.definition: Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance as a staged emotional trajectory.
emotional_trajectories.caution: Descriptively contested as psychology and clichéd as structure; useful mainly when a character resists the stages.

emotional_trajectories.name: cathartic release
emotional_trajectories.definition: Accumulated pity and fear are discharged at a single point, leaving the reader spent rather than happy.
emotional_trajectories.effect: The release is emotional, not situational: nothing needs to improve for catharsis to occur.

emotional_trajectories.name: bittersweet resolution
emotional_trajectories.definition: The external want is achieved and the internal one lost, or the reverse, so the close carries both signs at once.
emotional_trajectories.effect: The most durable ending shape in literary fiction because it refuses to round the number.

emotional_trajectories.name: eucatastrophe
emotional_trajectories.definition: A sudden joyous turn arriving after the situation has become genuinely hopeless.
emotional_trajectories.caution: Only legitimate if the hopelessness was played straight; hedged despair produces a turn nobody needed.

emotional_trajectories.name: revenge arc
emotional_trajectories.definition: Injury, pursuit, and the achievement of retribution, usually at a cost that exceeds the satisfaction.
emotional_trajectories.effect: The closing dip is what makes it an arc rather than a schedule of violence.

emotional_trajectories.name: bathos
emotional_trajectories.definition: An abrupt fall from the elevated to the trivial, whether as comic deflation or as failure of control.
emotional_trajectories.effect: Intentional bathos punctures pretension; unintentional bathos destroys the sentence that preceded it.
emotional_trajectories.register: comedy, satire; a hazard in earnest passages

hybrid_shapes.name: detective arc
hybrid_shapes.definition: Certainty rises as the investigation closes while the moral situation darkens, so the two curves run in opposite directions.
hybrid_shapes.effect: The reader gets epistemic satisfaction and emotional cost from the same ending.

hybrid_shapes.name: conversion narrative
hybrid_shapes.definition: Prior life, crisis, turning, and new life told so that certainty and fortune rise together at the turn.
hybrid_shapes.register: spiritual autobiography, recovery memoir, ideological memoir
hybrid_shapes.caution: The pre-conversion self must be rendered fairly or the turn persuades nobody who has not already turned.

hybrid_shapes.name: deconversion narrative
hybrid_shapes.definition: The mirror of conversion: a held certainty erodes under pressure and the narrator leaves the framework that supplied it.
hybrid_shapes.effect: Ends with modest recovered footing rather than a new certainty, which is what distinguishes it from a conversion in reverse.

hybrid_shapes.name: restitution narrative
hybrid_shapes.definition: Frank's illness shape: I was healthy, I am sick, I will be healthy again.
hybrid_shapes.register: illness and injury writing; also the default shape of institutional crisis communication
hybrid_shapes.caution: The culturally preferred shape, which is why it gets imposed on experiences that do not fit it.

hybrid_shapes.name: chaos narrative
hybrid_shapes.definition: Frank's anti-shape: events accumulate without sequence or hope, told as 'and then, and then'.
hybrid_shapes.effect: Hard to read by design; the formlessness is the testimony.
hybrid_shapes.caution: Nearly unpublishable at length — most writers frame a chaos section inside a shaped whole.

hybrid_shapes.name: quest illness narrative
hybrid_shapes.definition: Frank's third shape: the affliction is accepted and treated as a journey that yields something the well self could not have.
hybrid_shapes.caution: Slides easily into redemptive cliché; the boon has to be specific and unwelcome.

hybrid_shapes.name: expose arc
hybrid_shapes.definition: A concealed wrong is uncovered piece by piece, so certainty climbs while the reader's estimate of the world falls.
hybrid_shapes.caution: The documentary standard rises with the curve; the last third must be the most heavily sourced.

hybrid_shapes.name: case study arc
hybrid_shapes.definition: Situation, intervention, outcome, and generalization, with the particular carrying the weight of the claim.
hybrid_shapes.register: business writing, teaching cases, clinical and policy writing
hybrid_shapes.caution: One case supports an existence claim, not a frequency claim; state which you are making.

hybrid_shapes.name: transformation narrative
hybrid_shapes.definition: Explicit before-and-after built around a single hinge, with the before state rendered in enough detail to make the after measurable.
hybrid_shapes.caution: The most heavily commercialized shape in nonfiction; readers arrive pre-armed against it.

hybrid_shapes.name: cautionary tale
hybrid_shapes.definition: A fall narrated so that the reader can locate the avoidable decision that caused it.
hybrid_shapes.effect: Doubles as argument: the descent is a proof that the decision was wrong.
hybrid_shapes.caution: Hindsight makes the wrong turn obvious; if it was obvious then, the subject is a fool and the tale teaches nothing.

hybrid_shapes.name: exemplum
hybrid_shapes.definition: A short narrative deployed inside an argument as an instance of the rule being urged.
hybrid_shapes.caution: The story must fit the rule it is asked to carry; a memorable exemplum that fits loosely rewrites the argument in the reader's memory.

hybrid_shapes.name: underdog arc
hybrid_shapes.definition: A protagonist with visibly inferior resources closes the gap through cost rather than luck.
hybrid_shapes.caution: The disadvantage must remain real at the climax; a protagonist who becomes the favourite has left the shape.

hybrid_shapes.name: counterpoint arc
hybrid_shapes.definition: Two lines run in opposition, one rising as the other falls, and cross somewhere in the middle.
hybrid_shapes.effect: The crossing point is the book's thesis in dramatic form; place it deliberately.

hybrid_shapes.name: convergent strands
hybrid_shapes.definition: Separately launched lines are drawn together so that they collide at a single late scene.
hybrid_shapes.effect: Tension comes from the reader seeing the convergence before the characters do.
hybrid_shapes.caution: Every strand must earn its own pages; readers skim the one they like least and the convergence lands short.

hybrid_shapes.name: parallel arcs
hybrid_shapes.definition: Two or more lines with the same shape run side by side, inviting comparison rather than collision.
hybrid_shapes.effect: The variation between the strands carries the argument; identical strands waste the structure.

hybrid_shapes.name: nested arc
hybrid_shapes.definition: A complete inner arc is embedded inside an outer one, so the inner resolution changes the meaning of the outer.
hybrid_shapes.caution: The inner arc must matter to the outer frame; decorative nesting stalls the book at its centre.

hybrid_shapes.name: mice quotient nesting
hybrid_shapes.definition: Milieu, inquiry, character and event threads are opened and closed in reverse order, like nested brackets.
hybrid_shapes.effect: Gives a structural test for endings: a thread closed out of order leaves the reader with an unaccountable feeling of incompleteness.
hybrid_shapes.register: short fiction especially, where mis-nesting is most audible
